correctness.rationale: Finite support makes every real exponential tilt admissible. Writing the tilted characteristic function as e^(iat)H(re^(it))/H(r), any nonreal upper-half-plane zero of H would force zero modulus on the rest of its entire upper semicircle under monotonicity, contradicting polynomial finiteness. The nonnegative-coefficient polynomial has no nonnegative real zeros, so all roots must be strictly negative. Its normalized factors are Bernoulli PGFs; after any tilt each factor has squared modulus 1-2q(1-q)(1-cos t), strictly decreasing for 0<t<pi. In degree two, differentiate the exactly expanded squared modulus with respect to cos t to obtain p1(p0+p2)>=4p0p2 for ordinary monotonicity, while real roots require p1^2>=4p0p2. Exact-rational checks confirm the example and its unit-circle zero after tilt. The m=0 endpoint is treated separately. The code only checks exact finite examples; no computational extrapolation is used.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The necessary-condition claim can be restated as: a nonnegative-coefficient polynomial whose modulus is angularly nonincreasing on every positive-radius upper semicircle has no nonreal zero. Classical PF-infinity/strongly Rayleigh terminology characterizes negative-root polynomials, but does not by itself supply this angular-modulus converse. The focal paper proves the direction from Bernoulli factors to strong monotonicity, not the reverse.

value.rationale: Aamand et al. use strong monotonicity as a nontrivial assumption for tilted sharp point-probability estimates. The exact all-degree finite-support classification determines the complete scope of that hypothesis for bounded counts and prevents attempts to seek additional finite classes; the strict ordinary-versus-strong three-point distinction provides a sharp useful diagnostic. The result is a natural distributional class characterization, not a routine numeric recomputation or arbitrary slice; it does not claim a better local-limit constant.
